extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and parties to PTAB inter partes review proceedings (petitioners, patent owners, PTAB judges)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria applied by the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB) in evaluating petitions, claim construction, prior-art challenges (obviousness/anticipation), evidentiary motions, and procedural matters in an IPR final written decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for unpatentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioner has the burden of proving unpatentability by a preponderance of the evidence. 35 U.S.C. § 316(e). That burden never shifts to Patent Owner except in limited circumstances not present here (In re Magnum Oil Tools Intl., Ltd.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preponderance of the evidence is defined as 'the greater weight of evidence, evidence which is, more convincing than the evidence which is offered in opposition to it.' United States v. C.H. Robinson Co., 760 F.3d 1376, 1383 (Fed. Cir. 2014). The petitioner must establish each element of the challenge by this standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine a person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA) by reference to relevant education and practical experience (e.g., bachelor's degree in Computer Science/Electrical Engineering/related field and years of practical experience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articulation should be precise about education and experience (the Decision adopted Petitioner’s formulation of bachelor's degree plus two years practical experience rather than a vaguer 'at least' formulation). The defined POSITA is used in obviousness and claim-meaning analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard (Phillips/§282/37 C.F.R. §42.100(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the same claim construction standard as in a civil action under 35 U.S.C. § 282(b): construe claims according to the ordinary and customary meaning understood by a POSITA in the context of the specification, prosecution history, other claims, and extrinsic evidence. Phillips v. AWH Corp., 415 F.3d 1303 (Fed. Cir. 2005) (en banc) applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification is usually dispositive and the single best guide to claim meaning. Extrinsic evidence (expert testimony, dictionaries, treatises) is less significant than the intrinsic record. If an inventor acts as lexicographer, the specification must set forth that definition with reasonable clarity, deliberateness, and precision (Renishaw; Poly‑Am.). Only those claim terms in controversy need to be construed, and only to the extent necessary to resolve the controversy (Realtime Data v. Iancu).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constricted construction of disputed claim terms only as needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Only those claim terms that are in controversy need to be construed, and only to the extent necessary to resolve the controversy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board will not construe every term; it construes particular terms when parties dispute their meaning or when necessary to resolve obviousness/anticipation disputes. Adopt constructions that align with intrinsic record and controlling court constructions when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption of prior court claim construction when persuasive
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may adopt a district court's claim construction if it better aligns with the specification and the parties do not meaningfully dispute it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the Board adopted the district court’s construction of 'user profile' as 'a collection of settings and information associated with a user' because it fit the specification and Petitioner did not object. Parties' concessions in hearing or briefs may influence adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of specific claim term 'user profile'
rubrics_metrics.description: For this patent, 'user profile' is construed as 'a collection of settings and information associated with a user.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board favored the district court construction over a narrower dictionary-style proposal because the specification described dedicated user folders and hierarchical directories consistent with settings/information associated with a user; Petitioner expressly agreed to the district court's construction at oral argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of specific claim phrase 'the first group of video information being configured to allow a user to edit'
rubrics_metrics.description: This limitation is construed to mean at least that a user can modify which video information is a part of the first group of video information (i.e., user can edit membership of the group).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a party proposes a reasonable construction and the opposing party does not meaningfully contest it, the Board may adopt that construction for purposes of the proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness legal framework (Graham factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. § 103 if, considering the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art, the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious to a POSITA before the effective filing date. The inquiry relies on underlying factual determinations: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art; (3) level of skill in the art; and (4) secondary considerations (commercial success, long-felt need, failure of others, unexpected results). Graham v. John Deere Co., 383 U.S. 1 (1966).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply KSR v. Teleflex guidance: motivation to combine references can come from explicit teaching, implicit suggestion, market forces, or design incentives. The POSITA is 'a person of ordinary creativity, not an automaton.' Evaluate each Graham factor with supporting evidence and expert testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to combine/principle of obviousness under KSR
rubrics_metrics.description: Motivation to combine prior-art references may be found explicitly or implicitly in the references themselves, in market forces, in design incentives, or in any need or problem known in the field at the time of invention and addressed by the patent. A POSITA is not an automaton and may be motivated by convenience or obvious design choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board will consider common-sense reasons (e.g., user convenience, implementation ease, prevailing design practice) in assessing whether one of ordinary skill would have made the combination. However, assertions like 'often cheaper' must be supported with reasoning and evidence; nebulous assertions are less persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed publication/public availability of prior art (web materials)
rubrics_metrics.description: To use a reference as prior art, the petitioner must show it is a printed publication (i.e., publicly accessible) with a publication date prior to the patent's earliest effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For online/web materials, rely on documentary evidence and declarants regarding publication dates and public accessibility (e.g., declarations about web content dates). Lack of convincing evidence on publication date can render a purported reference inapplicable. Evidence relating solely to proving publication date can be subject to motions and evidentiary rulings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapping prior art to individual claim limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioner must account for each claim limitation by showing that prior art either expressly discloses the limitation or would have rendered it obvious in combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board reviews each limitation (including preamble when limiting) and examines whether prior-art references disclose or would have suggested that element; dependent claims are assessed in light of their parent claims. If an asserted reference fails to disclose a limitation, petitioner may rely on other references or combinations to fill the gap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing expert testimony and credibility of witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board evaluates the credibility and weight of expert declarations and testimony when experts disagree about facts (e.g., what a reference discloses or whether a reference is publicly available).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credibility determinations may be based on consistency with documentary evidence, reasoned explanations, and whether claimed factual positions are contradicted by explicit language in the cited references. The Board may discount expert testimony that is inconsistent with the intrinsic record or that lacks persuasive explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary motions (motion to exclude / motions to submit supplemental information)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may move to exclude exhibits or move to submit supplemental information; the Board will rule on admissibility and may deny motions to submit evidence or dismiss motions to exclude as moot if the evidence is not relied upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a motion to submit supplemental information is denied, those exhibits are not before the Board and cannot be considered in the decision. A motion to exclude can be dismissed as moot if the Board's conclusions do not rely on the evidence at issue. Parties should explain the basis for exclusion with specificity; unexplained exhibits may not affect findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of doctrines like issue preclusion/collateral estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may assert that prior decisions or findings preclude relitigation of issues (issue preclusion/collateral estoppel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board may consider whether preclusion applies but need not decide it if the decision can be reached on the merits without invoking preclusion. If applied, preclusion can bar a party from contesting matters already finally decided in prior proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural posture and statutory/regulatory authority for IPR decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Final Written Decisions in IPRs are issued pursuant to 35 U.S.C. § 318(a) and under Board procedures (e.g., 37 C.F.R. § 42.73); parties seeking judicial review must follow notice/service requirements (37 C.F.R. § 90.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent Owner is reminded of options for amendments post-decision (reissue or reexamination) and of continuing obligations to update mandatory notices (37 C.F.R. § 42.8). The Board’s decisions reference applicable statutes and rules throughout proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of claim priority/effective filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess priority chain and whether claims are entitled to the asserted earlier priority dates; effective filing date affects which version of statutes applies (AIA vs pre-AIA) and which prior art is relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claims are not entitled to an earlier priority date, the AIA versions of sections (e.g., 35 U.S.C. § 103) may apply. The Board may rely on findings from related proceedings about entitlement to priority when evaluating applicable prior art.
